extractor.note: Read every paragraph carrying transcend- (outside transcendental), immanen-, surpass or overstep, in file order. The Introduction's "transcendent height" (überschwängliche Höhe) and "transcendent expectations" are not the theme and are not recorded.

coverage_note: Term-led pass over the whole file (lines 1-770): every paragraph containing the transcendence family, including bare transcendent and immanent, was read; paragraphs without such a word were not read.

units.claim: What is given as being-for-me includes not only consciousness and its immanent contents but also what is foreign and external to the I.
units.quote: But the givenness extends beyond what is immanent to consciousness: what is "foreign" to the I, "external" to it, is also given through consciousness.

units.claim: Husserl draws the fundamental contrast between inner, immanent perception and outer, transcendent perception, with esse = percipi holding for the immanent sphere.
units.quote: Husserl now draws the fundamental contrast between inner (immanent) and outer (transcendent) perception.

units.claim: The outer-perceived gives itself as in-itself, contingent to being perceived, and as transcending the perception and the whole I-ish sphere.
units.quote: It thus gives itself as something for which being-perceived, having-been, and going-to-be are contingent — as in-itself over against the factual perceiving of the perceiving subject, as transcending the perception and with the perception the whole sphere of the I-ish.

units.claim: The possibility of error is structurally connected to the transcendence of the outer object, because the object claims to be in itself.
units.quote: The possibility of error (false perception, illusion) is structurally connected to this transcendence: because the object claims to be "in itself," the perception can be wrong about it.

units.claim: That the being of immanent experiences is exhausted in their being-conscious is a phenomenological description, not a metaphysical idealism.
units.quote: The being of immanent experiences is exhausted in their being-conscious (esse = percipi), but this must be understood carefully: it is not a metaphysical idealism but a phenomenological description.

units.claim: Immanent perception excludes modal modification while outer perception is susceptible to it, which establishes absolute evidence of the immanent against presumptive evidence of the transcendent.
units.quote: This analysis establishes the fundamental distinction between the absolute evidence of the immanent and the merely presumptive evidence of the transcendent.

units.claim: Objects called I-foreign, transcendent or outer are perceivable only as appearing and are what they are only as something appearing in appearances.
units.quote: We can straightforwardly say: they are what they are only as something appearing in appearances; for were they otherwise, perceptions would have to be thinkable in which they would bodily give themselves in their otherness.

units.claim: The object of immanent perception in principle cannot appear: the distinction between object and appearance is necessarily absent for it.
units.quote: For immanent perception, the distinction between the object itself and the appearance of the object is necessarily absent.

units.claim: Objects receive their sense as immanent or transcendent exclusively from the perceiving consciousness, so the distinction is constitutive rather than metaphysical.
units.quote: The objects' sense as immanent or transcendent is received from the perceiving consciousness — a key phenomenological thesis: the distinction is not metaphysical but constitutive.

units.claim: The outer object is essentially transcendent and never finally determined; not even God could perceive it adequately, and the thing remains in suspension between being and non-being.
units.quote: The concluding formulation — the thing remains "in suspension between being and non-being" — captures the essential precariousness of all transcendent positing.

units.claim: The distinction is crystallized as externality equals givenness through appearance and presumptive being, immanence equals givenness without appearance and absolute being.
units.quote: This paragraph crystallizes the fundamental ontological distinction in a pair of reversible propositions: externality = givenness through appearance = presumptive being; immanence = givenness without appearance = absolute being.

units.claim: Against the image-theory, an appearance is not a separate real thing but an immanent component of the perceptual experience, inseparable from the intentional relation.
units.quote: But an appearance is not a separate real thing at all — it is an immanent component of the perceptual experience itself, inseparable from the intentional relation to the appearing object.

units.claim: Following purely the sense of perception within immanence yields the principled possibility of the non-being of all outer objects, with being and non-being as indices of structures of perceptual courses.
units.quote: Purely following the sense, there resulted in immanence the principled possibility of the non-being of all outer objects, and it resulted that being and non-being are indices for certain structures of perceptual courses

units.claim: The apprehension of oneself as I-person is itself a transcendent positing, since the human being is given through appearances.
units.quote: But this "I-person" apprehension is itself a transcendent positing: the human being is an object given through appearances (through the body), subject to the presumptive character of all transcendent givenness.

units.claim: Even if the world does not exist, the stream of conscious experience continues unaffected in its immanent being.
units.quote: The world may not exist; but even if it does not, the stream of conscious experience continues unaffected in its immanent being.

units.claim: Even a fantasized centaur is transcendent in the relevant sense, so the exclusion must encompass all transcendent positings of actualities and pure possibilities.
units.quote: The exclusion must therefore encompass all transcendent positings — whether of actualities or of pure possibilities — to secure the purity of the phenomenological field.

units.claim: Husserl addresses the transcendence of the a priori and resolves it by distinguishing the a priori truth from the immanent experience of insight in which it is grasped.
units.quote: Husserl addresses the problem of the transcendence of the a priori itself.

units.claim: All transcendent realities and possibilities excluded by the reduction remain within the phenomenological field in a modified way.
units.quote: all that has been excluded by the reduction — all transcendent realities and possibilities — nonetheless remains within the phenomenological field in a modified way

units.claim: The fundamental question posed is how transcendent objectivity, under the titles nature and spirit, is given a priori as correlate of outer intuitions.
units.quote: how is transcendent objectivity (for which we have the still quite unclear titles "nature" and "spirit") given a priori as the correlate of outer intuitions?

units.claim: Supplement IV holds that an a priori truth is not a temporal event in the stream and in that sense transcendent, while the act of insight grasping it is immanent.
units.quote: But the conscious act in which the truth is grasped — the evidence, the insight, the judgmental experience — is immanent.

absences.expected_because: The return to prescientific consciousness is where the lectures turn to the pregiven as such, which the following sections divide into immanent I-own and transcendent I-foreign.
